newsitem.title: USA: High water closes more locks on upper Mississippi.
newsitem.headline: High water closes more locks on upper Mississippi.

text.p: High water fed by melting snow forced more lock closures on the upper Mississippi River near Minneapolis and south, further hampering river navigation, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers said.

"As of Thursday, we have had nine locks closed. Between Lock and Dam 6 (north of LaCrosse, Wis.) and the Twin Cities of Minneapolis and St Paul, Minn., navigation is shut down," said Peter Verstegen, public affairs specialist with the St Paul District, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.
"Everything from upper and lower St. Anthony Falls, Minn., and south to Lock and Dam 6 is closed," he added.
He added that two locks, Lock and Dam 5A (near Fountain City, Wis.,) and Lock and Dam 6 (near Trempealeau, Wis.) will be closed on Thursday.

"The crest will be moving down the river and we expect to close Lock and Dam 8 (Genoa, Wis.) on April 14, close Lock and Dam No. 9 (at Eastman, Wis.) on April 15 and Lock and Dam No. 10 (Guttenberg, Iowa) on April 16," Verstegen said.
"The Mississippi River at Minneapolis is forecast to crest Thursday at 17.5 feet and should be about 17.3 feet this morning. Flood stage is at 16 feet," he said.

The Mississippi River was running extremely fast, he said. But the recent cold wave sweeping across the upper Midwest slowed the snow melt near the Mississippi River and its tributaries as well as the Minnesota River, Verstegen noted.
"Right now, none of our locks and dams are closed, said Pat Ofslager, public affairs specialist, Rock Island District, Illinois. "But we are closely monitoring the situation."

Depending on weather and if tail water stages reach or exceed certain levels, "we would be closing some locks and dams on the Mississippi between Dubuque, Iowa (Lock and Dam 11) and Hannibal, Mo. (Lock and Dam 22)," Ofslager said.
Tail water is the level of the water below a dam.
U.S. exporters and grain dealers said they anticipate barge traffic will not resume normal operations for at least a month.
Cost Insurance Freight (CIF) values basis the U.S. Gulf in the nearby positions have firmed the past two days due to problems on the upper Mississippi, U.S. exporters and grain dealers said.
"It's the worst of both worlds for the barge industry," Ingram Barge Co marketing manager Jerry Knapper said.
Ingram is based in Nashville, Tenn.

"Operating costs are up because of all the navigational troubles on the lower and upper Mississippi River and nearby load demand has been deflated because of the prior price runup in grain prices," Knapper said.
Many elevators along the river have not been able to load, he said. Ingram is one of the key barge lines that operates in the St Paul, Minn. area.
"We are stuck for now," Knapper said.
